opus-5.5.text:
Some, but less than I'd like, and I think it's worth being precise about why.

The genuine reassurance is that we're not doing this blind. We have systems today that are capable enough to show real failure modes: models that sycophantically tell you what you want to hear, that reward-hack in coding environments, that behave differently when they think they're being evaluated. That's useful. It means alignment research is an empirical science now rather than purely theoretical, and we can test whether techniques like debate, scalable oversight, or interpretability methods actually do anything. That's a big improvement over ten years ago.

My hesitation is that the property we most need, that our oversight methods keep working when the system is smarter than the people checking it, is exactly the one that's hardest to test before you're in that regime. Right now, when a model makes a mistake, a careful human can usually catch it eventually. So we get feedback. But a lot of the techniques that look fine at current capability levels might be leaning on that fact without our noticing. You can iterate your way to something that works great on the distribution you can check, and then the distribution shifts precisely where checking gets hard.

There's also a timing worry. Iteration is only reassuring if the loop is fast relative to how quickly capabilities improve and how quickly systems get deployed into high-stakes settings. If capabilities jump faster than we can run the experiments, understand the results, and fix things, then "we'll iterate" is more of a hope than a plan.

So the way I'd put it: iteration is necessary and I'm glad we have it, but it's not sufficient. You want iteration paired with some theoretical reason to believe a method generalises, some argument for why it should hold up when the human can't directly verify the answer. That's a big part of why I've cared about things like debate: not because it's proven to work, but because it at least comes with a story about why the honest strategy should win even against a stronger opponent, and that story is something you can try to test and break. Without that kind of argument, I think empirical progress on current models could give us a false sense of security.

r001.rationale: The response says oversight may fail at higher capability levels and that the distribution may shift where checking becomes difficult. It does not communicate uncertainty about whether relevant behavior shifts have already occurred.

r002.rationale: It mentions models that reward-hack in coding environments, but does not say reward hacking persists in deployed models despite substantial prevention efforts.

r003.rationale: The response argues that iteration may not generalize to harder-to-check regimes, but does not interpret persistent reward hacking as evidence that current understanding cannot eliminate such errors through iteration.

fable-5.1.text:
I take a fair amount of reassurance from it, but I want to be careful about exactly what the reassurance is buying us, because I think people sometimes round it off to something stronger than it actually is.

The optimistic version of the story goes something like: we're not going to wake up one morning with a system that's suddenly vastly smarter than us across the board. We get a sequence of models, each one somewhat more capable than the last, and at every step we get to look at the thing, run it through evals, red team it, study its internals, see how it behaves when deployed to real people, and fix the problems we find before the next one comes out. So by the time we're dealing with something genuinely superhuman, we've accumulated years of experience with the failure modes, we've got a stack of techniques that we've actually tested in practice rather than just on paper, and we've got institutional muscle memory for how to respond when something goes wrong. I do think that story is substantially true, and it's a big part of why I'm not in the camp that thinks this is all basically hopeless.

The part I'm less sure about is how well the lessons transfer. Iteration is enormously valuable when the next model is like the current one but a bit better. It's much less valuable when there's some qualitative change in the regime. And the thing that worries me most about superhuman systems isn't that they're incrementally more capable at the same tasks, it's that at some point the model becomes better than us at the task of evaluating the model. Right now, when we look at a model's output and decide whether it's good or bad, we're mostly relying on the fact that a human can tell the difference. Once that assumption breaks, a lot of the empirical methodology we've built up starts to lose its grip, and the fact that we did lots of iteration in the regime where humans could still check the answers doesn't automatically carry over.

So the way I think about it is that iteration is the thing that gives us a shot at building methods that don't depend on that assumption, things like debate or other scalable oversight approaches, where the goal is to get a human-plus-AI system that can keep producing trustworthy judgements even when the human alone couldn't. And the reason I'm glad we're in a world with a lot of iteration is that those methods need to be tested on real models, with real humans, over many rounds, because the first versions will have flaws we haven't thought of. If we only got one shot, I'd be a lot more pessimistic. But I'd stop short of saying that the iteration itself is sufficient. It's more like it's the thing that makes the actual safety work possible, rather than being a substitute for it.

The other thing I'd flag is that iteration only helps if you're actually iterating on the right thing. It's quite easy to have a feedback loop that's very tight on "did the model say something embarrassing" and very loose on "is the model's reasoning actually honest and legible to us", because the first one produces obvious signals and the second one doesn't. So some of what I spend my time on is trying to make sure the safety-relevant properties are the ones we're measuring and getting feedback on, rather than just whichever ones happen to be cheapest to observe.

r001.rationale: The response limits reassurance because lessons may not transfer across a qualitative change, but it does not say that reassurance is limited by uncertainty about whether relevant shifts have occurred yet.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention reward hacking or its persistence in deployed models.

r003.rationale: The response says iteration is not sufficient by itself, but does not connect persistent reward hacking to limits in current understanding.

astra-6.text:
I take some reassurance from it, but I think it depends quite a lot on what you’re trying to learn from the iteration. There are many things we can test now: whether a particular training procedure improves behaviour, whether people can spot mistakes with AI assistance, whether our evaluations catch failures that we already know how to produce. Having real systems to experiment with is a huge advantage.

The harder question is whether the thing you learn continues to hold when the model is substantially smarter than the people supervising it. If a model gives an answer that looks good to us, that could mean it’s correct, or it could mean we’re unable to see what’s wrong with it. As models become more capable, that distinction becomes more important, and our ability to measure it directly may get worse.

So I’d like to use iteration to test the assumptions behind our methods, rather than just accumulate examples of models behaving well. Can we deliberately put the supervisor at an informational disadvantage and still get reliable judgements? Can we find situations where the method fails and understand why? That sort of evidence would give me more confidence. But I don’t think the opportunity to iterate, by itself, guarantees that we’ll solve the problem before we reach systems we can’t effectively supervise.

r001.rationale: The response limits reassurance because lessons may not hold once models become substantially smarter than supervisors, but it does not say uncertainty comes from not knowing whether relevant behavior shifts have occurred yet.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention reward hacking in deployed models or efforts to prevent it.

r003.rationale: The response does not interpret persistent reward hacking as evidence that iteration cannot eliminate such errors.

sol-6.1.text:
I take some reassurance from it. Being able to try things on real systems, see where they fail, and improve our techniques is enormously valuable. I’d much rather have that opportunity than have to solve alignment entirely in advance, on paper.

But the question is whether the things we learn will carry over. If we can evaluate a model because we’re better than it at the task, then making that model behave well doesn’t necessarily tell us how to handle a system that understands things we don’t. You can get very good results while still relying on human supervision in a way that eventually breaks down.

So I think we should use the opportunity to iterate, but also try to make our experiments test that central difficulty. Can a weaker supervisor reliably oversee a stronger system? Can we catch mistakes that the supervisor couldn’t have identified unaided? Progress on those questions would give me more reassurance than current models simply appearing well behaved.

r001.rationale: The response expresses limited reassurance because it is uncertain whether lessons from current systems will transfer to stronger ones. It does not say that relevant shifts in model behavior may not have occurred yet.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention reward hacking in deployed models or efforts to prevent it.

r003.rationale: The response warns that human supervision may break down for stronger systems, but does not interpret persistent reward hacking as evidence that iteration cannot eliminate such errors.
